claims.text: Define the term current account deficit (paragraph [2]) — define — 2 marks
What the question wants: a precise definition of a current account deficit that covers every item in the current account, not only goods.
What earned credit: "imports more goods than it exports" correctly identifies a deficit in trade, the largest part of the current account.
Provisional mark: 1 out of 2 — provisional
Biggest gap: the definition covers goods only.
The current account also includes trade in services, net primary income and net secondary income, so a deficit can come from any of them.
Fix it: 1) Name the current account and list what it covers.
2) Say what a deficit means for it: over a period, payments to the rest of the world exceed receipts from it.
3) Keep it to one or two sentences, with no example.

Model: "A current account deficit is when, over a period, a country's payments to the rest of the world on its current account (trade in goods and services, net primary income and net secondary income) exceed its receipts from the rest of the world on the same items."
Calculate the balance of trade in goods and services in 2025 — calculate — 2 marks
What the question wants: the 2025 balance of trade in goods and services, with the formula, the substitution and the unit.
What earned credit: the subtraction 45.6 − 55.1 is correct, and the answer carries its unit and a deficit sign.
Provisional mark: 0 to 1 out of 2 — provisional
Biggest gap: the question asks for goods and services, but your working uses goods only, so the services figures (15.3 and 10.4) are left out.
Fix it: 1) Write the formula with both items on each side: (exports of goods + exports of services) minus (imports of goods + imports of services).
2) Substitute all four 2025 figures from Table 1.
3) Compare your result with your own working in (c), where you add the goods balance and the services balance.
The two should agree.
Model: "Balance of trade in goods and services = (exports of goods + exports of services) − (imports of goods + imports of services)."
Calculate the 2025 current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP — calculate — 3 marks
What the question wants: the 2025 current account balance from its components, expressed as a percentage of 2025 GDP.
What earned credit: you list the components with the correct signs for net primary and net secondary income, and your arithmetic is correct for the figures you chose.
Provisional mark: 1 to 2 out of 3 — provisional
Biggest gap: foreign direct investment is an item of the financial account, which paragraph [2] of the text distinguishes from the current account.
Adding the 4.8 billion dalers of FDI inflow is the largest error.
The percentage also divides by 2024 GDP (412.0) rather than 2025 GDP (425.0).
Fix it: 1) Leave FDI out of the current account.
2) Use the 2025 GDP from Table 1 as the denominator.
3) Give the result with its unit and sign, to two decimal places, and with the percentage sign.
Model: "Current account balance = balance of trade in goods and services + net primary income + net secondary income."
Explain how the change in net exports from 2024 to 2025 affected real GDP, using an AD/AS diagram — explain — 4 marks

What the question wants: the direction in which the change in net exports shifts aggregate demand, the resulting change in the price level and real GDP, shown on an AD/AS diagram and linked to paragraph.
What earned credit: your net exports figures are correct on a goods and services basis (0.2 billion dalers in 2024 and −4.6 billion dalers in 2025), and your diagram uses the correct axes.

3) Use paragraph [3] to explain why net exports fell, quoting the figures.
4) End with the direction of the effect on real GDP.

claims.text: Assumptions: this is treated as HL, because parts (e) and (f) cover HL-only content; 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes and 1 Mbit = 10⁶ bits, following the question's convention.
Switch: forwards frames between the devices on the school's local area network, using MAC addresses, so local traffic goes only to the device it is addressed to.
Router: forwards packets between the local network and other networks, such as the school's internet connection to the cloud provider, using IP addresses.
1.8 GB × 1000 MB per GB = 1800 MB
1800 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 1.8 × 10⁹ bytes
1.8 × 10⁹ bytes × 8 bits per byte = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits
Upload speed 40 Mbit/s = 40 × 10⁶ bits per second = 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second
Time = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits ÷ 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second = 360 s
360 s ÷ 60 = 6.0 minutes
Answer: 6.0 minutes.
This is the minimum, because packet headers, acknowledgements and any retransmissions add data and slow the real upload.
6.0 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 6 000 000 bytes
6 000 000 bytes ÷ 1500 bytes per packet = 4000 packets
Answer: 4000 packets.
The division is exact, so no extra packet is needed.
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable.
Each segment is numbered and acknowledged, and any segment that is not acknowledged is sent again, so the server receives every part of the file.
TCP also uses the sequence numbers to reassemble segments in their original order.
UDP sends datagrams with no acknowledgement, no retransmission and no ordering, so packets lost on the connection would leave gaps in the video, and packets arriving out of order would scramble it.
A slower upload is acceptable, but a damaged file is not, so TCP's extra overhead is worth paying.
The file travels down the four layers on the school's computer, then up the four layers at the cloud server.
Application layer: the upload program gives the file to an application protocol, such as HTTPS, which adds its own header and passes the data down.
Transport layer: TCP divides the file into segments, adds a header with source and destination port numbers and sequence numbers, and passes each segment down.
Internet layer: IP adds a header with the school computer's IP address and the cloud server's IP address, creating packets.
Each router uses the destination IP address to forward the packet across the networks.
Network access layer: each packet is placed in a frame with the MAC address of the next device (the switch or router) and sent over the cable or wireless link.
At each hop the frame is replaced with one addressed to the next device, while the IP addresses stay the same.
At the cloud server, each layer removes its header in reverse order, and TCP reassembles the segments into the file for the upload program.
Compare asks for similarities only, so each point below is a similarity.
Both let the school's router choose the next hop for each packet bound for the cloud provider.
Both rely on a routing table, in which each entry matches a destination network to an outgoing route.
Both base the route on the destination IP address in each packet's header.
Both leave the end-to-end delivery to TCP, which resends any lost segment whichever route the packets take.
Static routes are entered by an administrator and do not adapt to failures, whereas dynamic routes are updated automatically by routing protocols.

claims.text: Por Marta Ruiz Salas, 2.º de Bachillerato
Cada verano, nuestra ciudad se llena de turistas que llegan con mapas en la mano, cámaras al cuello y muchas ganas de disfrutar.
Su presencia nos da trabajo y dinero, pero también nos obliga a preguntarnos quién se beneficia realmente de tanta actividad.
Algunos vecinos se quejan del ruido de la noche, del aumento de los alquileres y de unas calles tan llenas que apenas se puede caminar por ellas.
En estas líneas quiero analizar las ventajas y los inconvenientes del turismo y proponer dos medidas para que visitantes y vecinos convivan mejor.
Conviene empezar por lo positivo.
El turismo crea empleo en hoteles, restaurantes y comercios, y permite que pequeños negocios, como una panadería o una tienda de artesanía, sobrevivan durante todo el año.
Además, los visitantes ayudan a mantener museos, fiestas y monumentos que, de otro modo, quizá no tendrían recursos suficientes.
Para los jóvenes que trabajan en verano, es una oportunidad de ganar un dinero que les permite estudiar o ahorrar.
Sin embargo, los inconvenientes son reales y no se pueden ignorar.

Resulta preocupante que muchas familias no puedan pagar el alquiler de su propio barrio, porque numerosos pisos se alquilan a turistas durante el verano y dejan de estar disponibles para quienes viven aquí todo el año.
Tampoco es razonable que el ruido de las terrazas continúe hasta las tres de la madrugada, cuando hay vecinos que madrugan para ir al trabajo.
Y las calles abarrotadas hacen que los habitantes eviten los lugares que antes frecuentaban, como el mercado o la plaza de siempre, lo cual empobrece la vida cotidiana de la ciudad.
Algunos responderán que, sin turistas, la ciudad perdería ingresos y empleos.
Es cierto, pero el problema no es el turismo en sí, sino el modo en que se gestiona.
Si se concentrara en unos pocos meses y en unas pocas calles, resultaría muy difícil convivir; en cambio, si se repartiera a lo largo del año, sus beneficios llegarían a más barrios.
Para mejorar la convivencia, propongo dos medidas.
En primer lugar, sería necesario que el ayuntamiento limitara la concesión de nuevas licencias para pisos turísticos en los barrios residenciales.
De este modo, más viviendas quedarían disponibles para los vecinos que trabajan y estudian aquí todo el año, y el precio del alquiler dejaría de subir tan deprisa.
Mi segunda propuesta se centra en el ruido y en la masificación.
Sería útil que las terrazas cerraran a medianoche entre semana, para que los vecinos pudieran descansar, y que el ayuntamiento promoviera rutas turísticas por barrios menos conocidos.
Así, los visitantes descubrirían otros rincones de la ciudad y los lugares más concurridos podrían respirar un poco.
La convivencia entre vecinos y visitantes no es un problema imposible de resolver.
Envía tu propuesta al buzón de la revista antes del viernes.
